text: I pick a number from one to n, and you have to find it. You can call guess of num, which returns negative one if your guess is too high, one if it's too low, and zero if it's right. Return the number I picked.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the number never changes while I'm guessing, and it's guaranteed to be inside one to n. Is that right?
Let me also make sure I have the sign right, because it's easy to flip. One means my guess was too low, so the answer is bigger than what I said?
Yes. The return value describes your guess, not my number.
Good. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n can go up to two to the thirty-first, minus one.

That's a number I want to flag right away. Two to the thirty-first minus one is INT MAX, so any place where I add two candidate values together can overflow. I'll come back to that when I write the midpoint. The other thing I want to name early: guess is monotonic. If a guess is too low, everything below it is also too low. So the answers form one clean pattern — too low, too low, hit, too high, too high. That's a boundary, which means binary search.

Let me run through the example. Say n is ten and the pick is six. I guess five and get one, so one through five are gone. I guess eight and get negative one, so eight and up are gone. One more guess, and I land on six.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to call guess of one, guess of two, and so on. That's linear, and with n around two billion it's hopeless. This problem reminds me of plain binary search on a sorted array. The only difference is that I can't read the values — I can only ask the API. But binary search never needed an array. It needs a monotonic yes-or-no test, and guess gives me one. There's a choice in how to write it. The obvious version has three branches and returns early on zero. I want to fold it into two branches instead, and I'll explain why in the plan.

Here's the plan. Each round I ask only one yes-or-no question: was my guess too low? One: left and right mark a closed range that always holds the pick. Two: if mid is too low, left becomes mid plus one; otherwise right becomes mid. Three: when one cell is left, return it. One thing worth flagging — I'm merging too high and exact into the same line. Negative one means the pick is below mid; zero means it is mid. Both give pick less than or equal to mid, and right equals mid keeps mid in range. Shrinking to mid minus one could save a round, but it throws away an exact hit — I'll pay at most one extra round to drop a branch and a dead code path. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Left starts at one, right at n, and the loop runs while left is less than right. Each round calls guess exactly once — if the API were slow or metered, calling it twice would double the real cost. Too low moves left past mid; anything else sets right to mid. One thing worth flagging — the midpoint is left plus half of right minus left, never left plus right over two, because n can be INT MAX. And there's no return negative one at the bottom. In the three-branch version you're forced to write one for the compiler, but it can never run, since the pick is guaranteed to exist. Here the loop ends with exactly one candidate, so the dead line has nowhere to live.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. n is ten, pick is six, and I expect six. The last row is the interesting one: the range is six to seven, mid is six, and guess says zero. I hit the number and I don't return — I treat zero exactly like too high and set right to mid. That keeps six in range, so it becomes the only survivor, and return left hands it back. Four calls total. Let's also test with corner cases. n equals one: the loop never runs, so I return one with zero API calls. n two, pick two: mid rounds down to one, too low, one call. n at INT MAX with pick one: thirty-one calls. And pick INT MAX: thirty calls, returning INT MAX.

The time complexity is log n, and the meaningful unit here is API calls, not instructions — one guess per round. The space complexity is constant. In the worst-case scenario that's thirty-one calls at n equals two to the thirty-first minus one. And that's essentially optimal: each call splits the candidates around one point, so k calls can only tell apart about two to the k numbers. Oh, one more thing — back to the overflow point. When the pick is in the upper half, the second round already has left just over one billion and right at INT MAX. Left plus right over two wraps around to about negative five hundred thirty-seven million — a guess that isn't even in range, and the search stops converging. Left plus half the difference gives about one point six billion. Here it's the difference between working and not.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You proved the merge of too high and exact with one inequality — pick less than or equal to mid — instead of asserting it. You pointed out that the usual return negative one is unreachable and restructured the loop so it isn't needed. And you caught the overflow from the constraint alone, with the actual wrapped value to back it up. Good work.
